title: Polenta con Funghi
subtitle: soft polenta with a pan of sauteed mushrooms
excerpt: Polenta con funghi is soft, buttered polenta served with a topping of mushrooms sauteed in garlic, wine, and herbs. The polenta is the base; the mushrooms are the sauce. Serves 4.
sourceNotes: Polenta with mushrooms is one of the most common combinations in northern Italian cooking, particularly in the mountain regions of Lombardy, Veneto, and Piedmont. Pellegrino Artusi, La scienza in cucina (1891, public domain in Italy), includes mushrooms cooked in olive oil and wine as a standard preparation for serving with polenta or pasta. The combination of soft polenta and sauteed mushrooms is a practical dish that makes the most of the autumn mushroom harvest, using the soft polenta as both starch and sauce-absorber.

glossaryTerms.definition: Polenta cooked to a loose, flowing consistency suitable for serving from a spoon, rather than set firm. The ratio of water to polenta is higher (about 4:1 by weight) than for setting. Serve immediately; it firms quickly on cooling.

content.text: con funghi is two preparations served together: a pot of soft, buttered polenta and a pan of mushrooms sauteed in garlic, white wine, and thyme. The polenta goes into warm bowls; the mushrooms and their juices are spooned over the top. The combination is one of the most satisfying in northern Italian cooking: the polenta soaks up the mushroom juices as you eat.

Use whatever mushrooms are available. The dish works with chestnut mushrooms alone, improves with a handful of dried porcini added to the cooking liquor, and is excellent with wild mushrooms when in season. Arrange the cooking so the polenta finishes at the same time as the mushrooms: they both need to be served immediately.

items.prepNote: soaked in 150 ml hot water 20 minutes, chopped, liquid strained

content.text: Bring {{water}} of water to the boil with {{salt-table}} of salt. Whisk in {{polenta-coarse}} of polenta in a thin stream. Reduce heat and cook, stirring frequently, for the time on the packet (5 minutes for instant; 35 to 40 minutes for coarse). Finish by stirring in {{unsalted-butter}} of butter and Parmesan if using. Keep warm over the lowest heat.

Heat {{olive-oil}} of olive oil in a large saute pan over high heat. Add {{mushrooms-chestnut}} of chestnut mushrooms in one layer. Leave for 2 to 3 minutes until browned. Stir and cook 2 minutes more.

Add {{garlic}} of garlic and thyme. Cook 1 minute. Add soaked porcini and their strained liquid if using. Add {{dry-white-wine}} of white wine and let it bubble for 2 to 3 minutes until reduced. Season with {{sea-salt-fine}} of salt and {{black-pepper}} of black pepper.
Serve the polenta in warm bowls, spoon the mushrooms and their pan juices over the top, and finish with {{parsley-flat}} of parsley.

items.symptom: Polenta sets too firm while mushrooms cook
items.cause: Cooked too early or heat too high while waiting
items.fix: Keep the polenta over the lowest possible heat with a splash of water stirred in. Start cooking the mushrooms when the polenta has about 10 minutes left.

items.symptom: Mushrooms release water rather than browning
items.cause: Pan too crowded or not hot enough
items.fix: Use a large pan and high heat. Cook in two batches if necessary.

content.text: Polenta con funghi is the everyday meal of the northern Italian mountain kitchen in autumn. It appears on trattoria menus in the Dolomites, the Alps above Bergamo, and the Apennine foothills throughout October and November. The dish requires almost nothing in terms of technique: cook the polenta, saute the mushrooms, combine. It is the opposite of elaborate Italian cooking and is all the better for it. At home it is the kind of meal that can be on the table in under an hour, tastes as good as anything more complex, and uses whatever mushrooms happen to be available.
